# **One Unified Explore in Semantic Layer Is a Performance Liability, Not a Design Virtue**


[DV Engineering](https://medium.com/@dv-engineering?source=post_page---byline--57a6a3567063-----------------------------------------)


5 min read


·


1 day ago


--


*Written By:*[Marutha Sangeetha Shanmugam](https://www.linkedin.com/in/marutha-sangeetha-shanmugam-28b5a5101/)


If you’re a Data Engineer, Data Architect, BI Developer, or someone who’s ever stared at a slow dashboard and thought, “Why is this so painful?”, this one’s for you. Just a real problem, a relatable analogy, and the fix that actually worked.


I’ll reference Google Looker throughout this post. It’s what we run at DV. But swap in the dbt Semantic Layer, Cube.dev, Power BI, Tableau, or even a raw PostgreSQL view layer, the anti-pattern is identical. The tool doesn’t create the problem — the design does.


Alright, imagine this.


You’re cooking dinner for three different friends. One is vegan, one is keto, and one eats everything. So you cook three separate meals; it totally makes sense, right? Each one is perfectly tailored.


But then your sous chef walks in and says, *“* Hey, can you just pick a few things from the keto meal, a few from the vegan one, and a little from everything else, mix it all up so it’s a better-balanced diet for everyone?”


That’s basically what we were doing with our data pipelines.


## Here’s the Actual Situation — Semantic Layer Join


We have three separate data pipelines at work: ***Orders, Billing* , and *Shipments*** *.* Each one does its own thing. Different business logic, different data shapes. And as pipelines, they were really well designed. We’ve never faced any issues with reports or dashboards that run against an individual dataset.


But then came the reporting pressure. Stakeholders wanted **a single dashboard with multiple tiles and slide-outs** that required metrics from 3 different datasets. Makes sense from a business perspective. But here’s where things went sideways.


Instead of thinking hard about *how* to combine them properly, we just said, “Eh, let’s stitch them together in Looker.” Just create one big *Explore* .


It felt clean. It felt like good architecture. *It was not.* 🙃


## Why It Blew Up


Here’s what actually happens under the hood when you do that.


Every time someone loads a dashboard tile, even if they only care about *Shipments* data, the query engine touches all three datasets.


It’s like asking the waiter for your bill, but before handing it over, they go back and manually recalculate every single order from every table in the restaurant, just to figure out what *you* owe.


On top of that, the three datasets don’t speak the same “language.” Their grain sizes (the level of detail at which they store data) differ. So Snowflake has to do a lot of expensive on-the-fly math to make them agree. And our persistent derived tables (PDT- the pre-built summary tables) rebuild costs? They scale based on the biggest table in the join, not what you actually queried. So you’re paying for a full mansion renovation every time someone wants to repaint one wall.


We’re ignoring that **storing a pre-aggregated result costs** **a fraction of what recomputing it on every query costs.** Storage is cheap. Computation, especially at scale, is not cheap.


Caching doesn’t fix this. You can’t cache your way out of a bad design.


Caching optimizes execution. It does nothing to fix the design. If your schema forces every query to do unnecessary work, caching just means you’re doing that unnecessary work less often.


## So What’s the Fix?


Here’s the thing that is actually the right call:


**You decide *how* the data is combined at the pipeline layer before a single Looker (or semantic or reporting) layer view is ever written.**


Specifically:


- Figure out what grain each dashboard/report actually needs. The grain each surface needs is determined by its finest dimension combination.
- Build a purpose-scoped, pre-aggregated table for each reporting surface, whether that’s a visual dashboard, a self-serve export tool, an API, or an external platform integration *.*
- If you absolutely need data from all three pipelines combined, integrate them in Snowflake at the pipeline layer. Own it there, instead of in the semantic layer.
- Then let Looker just do Looker things, such as metric definitions, access control, and calculated fields, on top of data that’s **already clean and aggregated.**


Basically, **Looker is the finishing touch, not the construction site.**


## Okay, But Does It Actually Work? (Answer Is: Yes )


We ran a POC. Same data, same dashboard, two different approaches:


### Before: The “Just Stitch It in Looker” World


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Every time someone opened the dashboard, Snowflake was waking up, joining *Orders* + *Billing* + *Shipments* , resolving grain mismatches, and running CASE logic on the fly. Even for a simple “How many orders today?” tile.


### After: Purpose-Scoped Pre-Aggregated Tables


We built three lightweight pre-aggregated tables, one per pipeline, each pre-joined and rolled up to the reporting grain. Cross-dataset metrics got their own dedicated Snowflake aggregate, built at the pipeline layer. Looker’s job is just to read and display.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


### The Real-World Feel


Before the fix, analysts would open the dashboard, wait long enough, and *still* be loading. After? Users don’t see the architecture change. They just notice that suddenly everything feels fast. And that’s exactly the point.


## Takeaway


One big unified Explore *feels* like good design. It’s actually a performance liability. Design the aggregation contract upstream, and everything downstream gets cheaper, faster, and way easier to maintain.


Looker gave me the vocabulary to explain this problem clearly: Explores, PDTs, and derived tables. But the lesson isn’t about Looker. It’s about the contract between your pipeline and your reporting layer.


Whatever tool sits between your warehouse and your end user **should receive clean, pre-aggregated, grain-correct data. It should not be the place where that work happens for the first time.**


If your semantic layer is doing heavy lifting, that’s not a sign of a powerful semantic layer. That’s a sign of an upstream design gap.


That’s it. That’s the whole story. 🎉
